No, that doesn't mean that they "made up deaths:" mortality reporting lags behind real-time; every mortality dataset the CDC publishes comes with that footnote or disclaimer. They say themselves that numbers may "lag" as many as 8-10 weeks:

"Data during this period are incomplete because of the lag in time between when the death occurred and when the death certificate is completed, submitted to NCHS and processed for reporting purposes. This delay can range from 1 week to 8 weeks or more, depending on the jurisdiction, age, and cause of death." meaning that a significant quantity of death reports take 8-10 weeks to get to the CDC. When they arrive, the CDC will update the death count for the week the death happened, not the week that the report was received. https://data.cdc.gov/NCHS/Provisional-Death-Counts-for-Coronavirus-Disease-C/hc4f-j6nb

Mortality reporting came in.

This happens every week, to every week within the last ~15 weeks. Every week when the CDC publishes their updated numbers, some deaths will almost certainly be added to each of the last ~15 or so weeks. The amount that gets added depends on how many people actually died in those weeks; those death certificates have been taking their time working their way from wherever the person died, to the CDC.

The CDC says 8-10 weeks maximum lag, and they intentionally don't even report the most-recent 2 weeks to avoid confusion because those weeks' numbers are always so low compared to what they'll end up being. I use 15 weeks because that's when the numbers seem to really stop moving.
